extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in literary theory and Stanley Fish
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biography summarizing Stanley Fish's life, career, major ideas (especially reader-response/interpretive communities), public positions, criticisms, and bibliography. Useful for readers seeking an overview of his theoretical stances and controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of a text is dependent upon each reader's own subjective experience in one or more communities, each of which is defined as a 'community' by a distinct epistemology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard: an interpretation should be understood in terms of the epistemic conventions of the reader's interpretive community; critics should attend to communal norms when judging readings. (Original phrasing: 'interpretive communities' — an offshoot of reader-response criticism — examines how the interpretation of a text is dependent upon each reader's own subjective experience in one or more communities, each of which is defined as a 'community' by a distinct epistemology.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic competence as basis for constrained interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A reader's subjective experience is valuable (i.e., 'constrained' rather than idiosyncratic) insofar as it rests on an internalized, shared linguistic competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criterion: distinguish between uncontrolled idiosyncratic responses and constrained, communicable interpretations by checking whether the reading relies on shared linguistic norms/competence. (Page notes Fish borrows the linguistic notion of 'linguistic competence' — 'the idea that it is possible to characterize a linguistic system that every speaker shares.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of interpretation derives from community norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Textual authority and the legitimacy of interpretations come from the conventions and practices of interpretive communities rather than from an objective, author-centered meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating criticism, emphasize how community standards establish what counts as a defensible reading; consider Fish's book title: 'Is There a Text in This Class? The Authority of Interpretive Communities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrained vs uncontrolled subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: An interpretation is 'constrained' (and thus valuable) when it is tied to shared, normative boundaries rather than being an uncontrolled assertion of individual taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess interpretations by whether they can be justified within communal norms and linguistic competence; anti-pattern is treating any subjective response as equally valid without showing constraint or shared grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly statements and university speech should be limited to professional expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities and faculty bodies should refrain from making political statements on matters outside their professional areas of expertise; Fish criticizes political statements by universities/faculty outside professional competence and has supported campus speech codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating institutional or faculty utterances, check for relevance to professional expertise; Fish's position implies a normative standard that institutional speech be professionally grounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanities valued intrinsically, not instrumentally
rubrics_metrics.description: The humanities have intrinsic worth and are not justified by instrumental utility; attempts to justify them from external purposes diminish their value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a criterion for programmatic arguments about humanities, prioritize intrinsic value claims rather than external instrumental defenses. (Page quotes Fish: 'To the question "of what use are the humanities?", the only honest answer is none whatsoever... The humanities are their own good.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Free speech judgments should consider the purpose and limits of free speech (e.g., malicious libel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses of free speech should be evaluated against the claimed purpose (e.g., the idea that free speech promotes discovery of truth); if the purpose does not cover malicious libel, defending libel in the name of free speech is incoherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adjudicating free-speech claims, assess whether the action defended (e.g., malicious libel) coheres with the asserted public goods of free speech; Fish uses Hustler Magazine v. Falwell as an example where defending deliberate malicious libel in the name of truth-seeking is problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness, impartiality, and reasonableness as critical expectations (critics' standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics of Fish argue that scholarship and public argument should adhere to fairness, impartiality, and reasonableness; rejecting these is grounds for critique (Judith Shulevitz's critique).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating essays or public intellectual work, consider whether the author observes norms of fairness and impartiality; critics label their absence an important defect (Shulevitz: Fish 'rejects wholesale the concepts of "fairness, impartiality, reasonableness."').

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarship should serve truth and exhibit logical rigor (critics' standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several critics charge that good scholarship requires placing learning in the service of truth, maintaining logical rigor, and using normative standards of argumentation rather than sophistry or radical relativism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should examine whether arguments are logically coherent, seek truth rather than merely rhetorical victory, and avoid sophistry; critics cited include R. V. Young, Terry Eagleton, Martha Nussbaum, and David Hirsch, each emphasizing truth-serving scholarship, logical rigor, or normative adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing the critic's values on a text (anti-pattern highlighted by critics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue that one should not presuppose readers (or critics) find an author's beliefs inimical and thereby wrest the text to the critic's own cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative caution: ensure interpretations allow for the possibility that readers and authors may share values; John Mullan's critique of Fish's Milton readings warns against readings that leave 'no room to consider that Milton's poetry might be wise about human weakness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical precision and adherence to argumentative standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Good criticism and scholarship require careful rhetorical precision and attention to standards of argumentation; lapses are grounds for censure (David Hirsch's and Nussbaum's critiques).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing criticism, aim for precise wording, clear logical moves, and explicit standards for adjudicating competing arguments; anti-patterns include 'lapses in logical rigor' and 'carelessness toward rhetorical precision.'
